title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Return the maximum of every window of size k using a monotonic deque in O(n).

data.text: Given an array `nums` and a window size `k` that moves from left to right, return an array of the maximum value in each window.
Take the max of every window independently. This is O(n·k) and re-scans elements that were already compared.

data.title: Brute Force O(n·k)
data.content: Scan each window for its maximum.

data.text: Maintain a deque of **indices** whose values decrease from front to back. The front is always the maximum of the current window. When a new value arrives, pop everything smaller from the back — those values can never be the maximum again — then push the new index. Finally, drop the front if it has fallen out of the window.

data.title: Monotonic Deque O(n)
data.content: Each index is pushed and popped at most once.

data.title: Store indices, not values
data.text: You need indices to know when an element leaves the window. Storing only values forces you to search for the departing element, which destroys the O(1) amortised cost.

data.title: Compare with >= to keep the newest equal value
data.text: Popping when `nums[back] <= nums[i]` (rather than `<`) replaces equal values with the newer index. Either comparison yields the correct maximum, but replacing keeps indices fresh so the window-expiry check fires less often.

data.caption: The deque holds a decreasing sequence of indices; the front is always the current window maximum.

cards.title: Scan each window
cons: Too slow for large n and k

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: A monotonic deque is the standard tool for 'maximum/minimum over a sliding range'. The same structure powers 'shortest subarray with sum at least k' and the min-stack variant of this problem.
